issues.legal_issue: A purchaser seeking specific performance must prove personal readiness and willingness through competent evidence, and an agent without personal knowledge cannot ordinarily prove the purchaser’s state of mind or conduct.
material_facts: The purchaser did not testify about his readiness and willingness to complete the sale.

The agent who testified for the purchaser was appointed after the relevant events and acknowledged that he had no personal knowledge of the transaction or of the purchaser’s readiness and willingness.
A different agent had negotiated and executed the agreement, and that agent was not examined.

The property dealer’s evidence could not establish the purchaser’s personal finances or intentions, and the facts did not establish that the purchaser’s affairs were entirely managed by an agent in a way that justified the recognized exception.
issues.conclusion: The purchaser failed to prove readiness and willingness as required for specific performance, and the suit for that relief had to fail.
issues.legal_principle: Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 requires both pleading and proof that the plaintiff performed or was always ready and willing to perform the essential terms of the contract. Readiness and willingness concern the purchaser’s state of mind, conduct, capacity, and preparedness. Under Order III, Rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure, an agent may testify about acts or transactions within the agent’s personal knowledge, but ordinarily cannot testify in place of the principal about matters known personally only to the principal. The Court relied on N.P. Thirugnanam v. R. Jagan Mohan Rao, Pushparani S. Sundaram v. Pauline Manomani James, Manjunath Anandappa v. Tammanasa, Vidhyadhar v. Manikrao, Janki Vashdeo Bhojwani v. Indusind Bank Ltd., and Shankar Finance & Investments v. State of Andhra Pradesh.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and principal_did_not_testify_on_readiness and testifying_agent_lacked_personal_knowledge and transaction_agent_was_not_examined and not exclusive_agent_management_exception

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding seeks specific performance of a contract.
predicates.principal_did_not_testify_on_readiness: The purchaser did not give evidence about the purchaser’s own readiness and willingness to perform.
predicates.testifying_agent_lacked_personal_knowled: The agent who testified lacked personal knowledge of the relevant transaction or the purchaser’s readiness and willingness.
predicates.transaction_agent_was_not_examined: The agent who handled the relevant transaction was not examined as a witness.
predicates.exclusive_agent_management_exception: The purchaser’s affairs were entirely managed by an agent in circumstances that could justify accepting the agent’s evidence about the purchaser’s readiness and willingness.

issues.definition: When a specific-performance plaintiff does not testify about readiness, the testifying agent lacks personal knowledge, the transaction agent is not examined, and the exclusive-management exception does not apply, readiness and willingness are not proved.

issues.legal_issue: A contractual provision for damages does not by itself exclude specific performance unless the agreement clearly makes monetary payment an exclusive remedy or gives the party in default an option to pay money instead of performing.
material_facts: The agreement did not expressly provide for specific performance or expressly bar it.
The agreement provided for payment of damages if the vendor defaulted and forfeiture of earnest money if the purchaser defaulted.
The damages provision did not give the vendor an option to pay money in lieu of performing the sale.
issues.conclusion: The damages provision did not prevent the purchaser from seeking specific performance, subject to proving the vendor’s breach and the purchaser’s readiness and willingness.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 10, 21(2), 21(5), and 23 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 permit specific performance where the statutory requirements are met, even if the contract names an amount payable on breach and does not separately provide for specific performance. Under Section 23, a named sum bars specific performance only where the contract shows that the sum gives the defaulting party an option to pay money instead of performing; compensation may otherwise be considered under Section 21 where specific performance is refused and compensation has been claimed.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and contract_names_damages_for_breach and not contract_makes_money_an_exclusive_remedy

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding seeks specific performance of a contract.
predicates.contract_names_damages_for_breach: The contract specifies a monetary consequence for breach.
predicates.contract_makes_money_an_exclusive_remedy: The contract clearly makes payment of money the exclusive remedy or gives the defaulting party an option to pay instead of performing.

issues.definition: A damages provision does not preclude specific performance when the proceeding seeks that relief, the contract names damages for breach, and the contract does not make payment an exclusive alternative to performance.

issues.legal_issue: A purchaser’s obligation to prove readiness and willingness is distinct from whether the vendor breached, and a vendor’s breach does not excuse the purchaser from proving that obligation.
material_facts: The purchaser argued that the vendor had not obtained clearances required for the sale and that the purchaser therefore did not need to prove readiness and willingness.
The Court treated vendor breach as a distinct question from the statutory bar against granting specific performance to a plaintiff who fails to prove readiness and willingness.
The evidence showed that the property dealer acting for the purchaser had been entrusted with obtaining the clearances and had called the vendor’s representative to complete the sale.
issues.conclusion: Even assuming that the vendor breached the agreement, the purchaser was barred from specific performance because he failed to prove that he was ready and willing to perform his own essential obligations.
issues.legal_principle: Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 bars specific performance where the plaintiff fails to aver and prove performance or continuing readiness and willingness to perform essential terms to be performed by the plaintiff, except terms whose performance was prevented or waived by the defendant. The Court distinguished the question of a defendant’s breach, which may give rise to a cause of action, from the separate personal bar to specific performance imposed on the plaintiff.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and purchaser_failed_to_prove_readiness and vendor_breach_is_alleged and purchaser_performance_was_not_prevented_or_waived

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding seeks specific performance of a contract.
predicates.purchaser_failed_to_prove_readiness: The purchaser did not prove readiness and willingness to perform the purchaser’s essential obligations.
predicates.vendor_breach_is_alleged: The purchaser alleges that the vendor breached the contract.
predicates.purchaser_performance_was_not_prevented_: The purchaser’s own performance was not shown to have been prevented or waived by the vendor.

issues.definition: In a specific-performance suit, an alleged vendor breach does not remove the bar to relief when the purchaser has not proved readiness and the purchaser’s performance was not prevented or waived.

issues.legal_issue: A purchaser who cannot complete the purchase when performance is due and whose conduct shows a failure to proceed commits a breach under an agreement that provides for forfeiture of earnest money on purchaser default.
material_facts: The vendor’s representative testified that the purchaser said on the agreed completion date that the full sale price was not available.
The purchaser did not purchase the required stamp paper that day, and the evidence that he had funds or assets did not establish that the money was available for the purchase.
The vendor’s representative’s account was unrebutted because the purchaser did not testify.
Contemporaneous correspondence supported the vendor’s account and indicated that the purchaser was not ready to complete on the scheduled date or the extended date.
The agreement provided that the purchaser’s earnest money would be forfeited if the purchaser failed to complete the sale.
issues.conclusion: The purchaser committed the breach, the earnest money stood forfeited, and he was not entitled to its refund.
issues.legal_principle: Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 requires proof of the purchaser’s readiness and willingness, including capacity and preparedness to perform the contract. The Court assessed the purchaser’s conduct and the surrounding evidence and applied the agreement’s term providing for forfeiture upon purchaser default.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and purchaser_could_not_pay_when_performance_was_due and purchaser_did_not_take_steps_to_complete and evidence_supports_purchaser_default and contract_provides_forfeiture_on_purchaser_default

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding seeks specific performance of a contract.
predicates.purchaser_could_not_pay_when_performance: The purchaser lacked the funds required to complete the purchase when performance was due.
predicates.purchaser_did_not_take_steps_to_complete: The purchaser failed to take steps required to complete the transaction when performance was due.
predicates.evidence_supports_purchaser_default: Unrebutted testimony or contemporaneous evidence supports the finding that the purchaser failed to proceed with completion.
predicates.contract_provides_forfeiture_on_purchase: The contract provides for forfeiture of earnest money if the purchaser defaults.

issues.definition: A purchaser’s failure to pay and take steps to complete, supported by the evidence, entails forfeiture when the contract provides for forfeiture on purchaser default.

issues.legal_issue: A stated completion date is not treated as essential when the parties’ conduct shows that performance was contemplated after that date.
material_facts: Although the agreement specified a completion date, the vendor’s representative was willing to complete the sale nearly six months later.
The parties continued to pursue completion after the date stated in the agreement, including arranging for the vendor’s representative to attend for registration.
issues.conclusion: Time was not of the essence of the contract.
issues.legal_principle: Whether time is essential is assessed from the agreement and the parties’ conduct. The Court inferred from the vendor’s willingness to perform after the stated date and the parties’ continued efforts to complete that time was not of the essence.

predicates.sale_contract_has_stated_completion_date: The sale contract specifies a date for completion.
predicates.vendor_willing_to_perform_after_that_dat: The vendor remained willing to complete after the specified date.
predicates.parties_continued_to_pursue_completion: The parties continued to take steps toward completion after the specified date.

issues.definition: A stated completion date is not essential when the vendor remains willing to perform afterward and the parties continue pursuing completion.
